pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: You rename `--output` to `--out`, add a `verify` subcommand, and fix a wrong exit code. Which version bumps does each one force, and why?
expected_points: renaming a flag breaks existing invocations — major
a new subcommand is additive — minor
the exit-code fix changes something scripts branch on, so it is major (or patch only if the old code was undocumented/plainly broken) — the learner should reason about the promise, not recite a table
a CLI's public API is its commands, flags, exit codes, machine-readable output shape and config keys — not its human-readable wording

questions.prompt: How does the version number get into a released binary, and what happens when you mistype the `-X` symbol path?
expected_points: go build -ldflags "-X <full import path>.<var>=<value>" overwrites a package-level string var at link time
the target must be a var (not a const) initialised to a constant string; in a subpackage the path is the module path plus the directory, not main
a wrong symbol path is silently ignored: the build succeeds and ships the placeholder
the defence is running --version in the pipeline and asserting on its output

questions.prompt: Explain what `CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=windows GOARCH=arm64 go build` needs installed on your machine, and why Go can do that when C toolchains struggle.
expected_points: nothing extra — no cross compiler, no system linker, no target headers
the Go compiler/linker target every platform and the runtime plus standard library are compiled from source for the target
the condition is pure Go: cgo would need a C compiler for the target, so CGO_ENABLED=0
the payoff is a static binary that runs on any distro or a scratch container; go tool dist list shows the pairs

questions.prompt: You push the tag `v1.4.2` and CI runs goreleaser. Walk me through what it does, and where the version string comes from.
expected_points: the version comes from the git tag ({{ .Version }} is the tag without the leading v); a dirty tree or a missing tag makes it refuse
builds the goos/goarch matrix with the configured flags and ldflags templates
archives the binaries, writes checksums.txt, generates release notes from commit subjects since the previous tag
creates the release and uploads the artifacts, then publishes downstream packages such as the Homebrew formula

questions.prompt: What exactly is a Homebrew tap, what does the formula for a Go tool contain, and what does goreleaser do about it?
expected_points: a tap is a git repo named homebrew-<something> under your account; brew install you/tap/digest resolves to it
the formula is Ruby: for a prebuilt binary it holds the release archive URL per platform, its sha256, and an install step copying the binary into bin
the brews: block generates and commits that formula after a successful release, with URLs and checksums filled in
it needs a token with write access to the tap repo — a different credential from the release token; homebrew-core would mean review and notability rules

questions.prompt: A user installs your tool with `go install example.com/digest@v1.4.2` — no goreleaser involved. What does `--version` print, and how did you arrange that?
expected_points: your ldflags never ran, so the vars still hold their placeholders
runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo gives bi.Main.Version (v1.4.2 here) and vcs.revision / vcs.time settings
precedence: linker flags, then build info, then placeholder
(devel) and empty are not real versions, so a plain local build still says dev

questions.prompt: Two builds of the same commit produce different bytes. Name the likely causes and what each fix is — and say why anyone should care.
expected_points: absolute paths from the build machine — fix with -trimpath
a wall-clock timestamp in ldflags — stamp the commit date instead
a different Go toolchain version — pin it; archive file timestamps — mod_timestamp
reproducibility lets anyone check that the published binary corresponds to the published source; checksums detect tampering in transit, signatures are what prove origin
